title: When Should You Use Slotted Deflection Track?
description: Learn when slotted deflection track is needed, distinguish vertical deflection from drift, and verify movement, ratings, gaps, and installation before you.
html:
Use slotted deflection track when a non-load-bearing interior partition must accommodate expected vertical movement between the structure above and the wall. Do not select it from wall height alone: the required movement, head-of-wall gap, track capacity, and any fire, acoustic, seismic, or drift requirements must come from the project documents and coordinated assembly.

The decision in one minute

Start with the wall’s structural role and the direction of movement. Slotted deflection track is generally appropriate when the wall carries no load from the structure above, but the supporting slab, beam, deck, or roof may move vertically relative to the partition.

  • Use a movement-accommodating head detail when the structural drawings or specifications identify vertical deflection that the partition must tolerate.
  • Use standard track when the wall detail does not require relative vertical movement and the connection is intended to remain fixed.
  • Escalate the design review when the wall must accommodate horizontal drift, seismic movement, load transfer, or a tested fire or acoustic condition.
  • Do not use a universal height rule. A 12-foot threshold is not a reliable substitute for the structural movement requirement.

The design team determines the movement demand. The installer and supplier then need to match that demand to the track’s allowable movement, slot geometry, stud engagement, fasteners, head gap, and complete wall assembly.

What slotted deflection track is designed to do

Slotted deflection track is a head-of-wall component for a non-load-bearing partition. Its slots and connection detail allow the structure above to move vertically without forcing that movement into the studs, gypsum board, or finished partition.

The track does not turn a partition into a load-bearing wall. The studs must be detailed and fastened so they remain engaged with the track while being able to move in the intended direction. A screw, board attachment, sealant joint, or adjacent framing connection that locks the head of the wall can defeat the purpose of the system.

Dimensions vary by product and approved assembly. As one Canadian public specification example, a slotted top runner is described with 63 mm downstanding legs, 6 mm wide by 38 mm high slots, and slots spaced at 25 mm on centre. Those dimensions describe that specified application, not a universal requirement for every project or manufacturer. Review the Canadian specification example for its stated context.

In practical terms, the track is slotted, but the slots do not by themselves establish movement capacity. Slot length, fastening location, stud clearance, track leg geometry, and installation gap work together. The selected product documentation and project detail control the usable range.

When should you use slotted deflection track?

Use slotted deflection track when all three conditions are present: the partition is non-load-bearing, the supporting structure is expected to move vertically relative to the wall, and the project detail requires that movement to be accommodated at the head of the partition.

Conditions that point toward vertical deflection track

  • A non-load-bearing partition runs from the floor to the underside of a slab, beam, joist, roof deck, or other structure that can deflect.
  • The structural drawings identify a vertical movement or deflection allowance at the partition location.
  • The architectural or partition details call for a deflection head, slip head, slotted track, or equivalent movement detail.
  • The wall is beneath a structural frame where loading, span, construction sequence, or occupancy may cause movement after the partition is installed.
  • The wall finish must remain separated from movement in the structure above.

Concrete frames, structural steel floors, composite decks, and other primary structures can all create this condition. The material of the structure does not decide the track selection by itself. The expected movement and the wall’s required performance do.

Movement conditions that need separate attention

Vertical structural deflection is the ordinary reason to investigate slotted deflection track. It concerns the structure moving toward or away from the partition in the vertical direction.

Horizontal drift or seismic movement is different. A vertical deflection product should not automatically be treated as a drift-capable or seismic system. If the wall must move laterally, the project may require a different head detail, side connection, clip, bracing arrangement, or engineered system.

Thermal movement, construction tolerances, shrinkage, vibration, and differential movement can also affect a partition. These conditions may overlap with vertical movement, but they do not automatically justify the same track. Identify the movement direction, magnitude, frequency, and connection requirements before choosing the product.

Load transfer is a separate issue. If the wall is intended to support gravity, wind, diaphragm, or other design loads, a nonstructural slotted track detail is not an automatic solution. The structural framing system and its design documents must govern.

Why wall height is not a universal trigger

Wall height can affect flexibility, stud selection, and the consequences of movement, but it does not establish a universal requirement for slotted track. Two walls of the same height can have different head details because they sit under different spans, loads, structural systems, or rated assemblies.

Look for the movement criterion in the structural drawings and specifications. One Canadian public tender requires designated partition heads to accommodate the minimum structural deflection shown on the structural drawings and gives L/360 as a stated example. That is a project criterion, not a blanket rule for every partition. See the tender’s head-of-partition requirement.

Standard track, slotted track, slip track, and drift systems compared

These terms are related, but they should not be treated as interchangeable product specifications. “Slip track” is often used broadly for a head-of-wall detail that allows relative movement, while the exact track, slot arrangement, fastener method, and tested assembly still need confirmation.

OptionMovement focusTypical wall roleWhat must be confirmed
Standard trackFixed connection, with no designed relative movement at the headNon-load-bearing partition where the project detail does not call for movement accommodationStud fit, gauge, dimensions, fastening, and wall requirements
Slotted deflection trackPrimarily vertical movement between the structure above and the partitionNon-load-bearing partition beneath a structure expected to deflectAllowable movement, slot dimensions, leg size, gap, stud engagement, and assembly documentation
Slip trackRelative movement, but the term may describe several product or detail arrangementsHead-of-wall movement detail specified by the projectExact product definition, movement direction, installation method, and tested or engineered detail
Drift-capable or seismic systemHorizontal movement, story drift, seismic movement, or combined movementWalls requiring lateral movement accommodation or a project-specific structural connectionDesign movement, direction, cycling, side connections, fasteners, and engineering documentation

The key distinction is movement direction. A track selected for vertical deflection should not be substituted for a system designed to accommodate horizontal drift unless the project documentation specifically supports that use.

How to read the movement requirement and head-of-wall gap

Find the controlling information in structural drawings, architectural wall details, specifications, and fire or acoustic assembly documentation. Record the wall’s structural role, expected movement, required head gap, track type, stud system, and performance requirements before requesting a quotation.

Connect the movement value to the product

The expected movement must be within the selected track system’s allowable movement. Review the slot length, slot orientation, permitted fastener location, track leg dimensions, stud engagement, and stated installation clearances. A longer slot does not automatically prove that the entire wall assembly can accommodate the movement.

The head-of-wall gap is the space that allows the assembly to move as designed. There is no universal gap value. The drawings, specification, selected system, and required movement govern it. The gap must be compatible with the approved joint treatment and must not be improvised in the field.

Separate beam deflection from wall deflection

When a structural drawing gives a limit such as L/360, that value describes a structural design criterion for the relevant member or condition. It is not automatically the movement capacity of the track or the exact gap to leave at the wall head.

Ask the design team to identify the movement that the partition head must accommodate, including construction, dead-load, live-load, or staged-loading assumptions. The track selection should respond to that partition-specific movement requirement.

Worked example: matching a wall detail to project movement

The following is hypothetical and illustrates the selection process. It is not a product recommendation or a universal design value.

Suppose a six-metre-high non-load-bearing partition sits below a structural floor. The engineer’s detail identifies 12 mm of downward movement that the head of the wall must accommodate. The architectural detail specifies a 20 mm head gap, and the partition has a required fire rating.

  1. Reject standard track for this location. A fixed head connection would not provide the specified vertical movement allowance.
  2. Check the proposed slotted track. Confirm that its documented allowable vertical movement is at least 12 mm under the stated installation conditions. Do not infer capacity from nominal track width.
  3. Check the slot and fastener detail. Verify slot length, slot spacing, fastener location, track legs, stud engagement, and stud-profile compatibility.
  4. Preserve the specified gap. The 20 mm gap belongs to this hypothetical detail. It is not a value to apply to another project.
  5. Coordinate the fire-rated assembly. Confirm that the selected track, joint width, sealant or other joint treatment, gypsum board, studs, and installation method belong to the same tested or labelled assembly.
  6. Inspect before closing the wall. Check that fasteners, board, insulation, sealant, services, and adjacent construction do not restrain the required movement.

If the proposed product cannot document the movement capacity, compatible stud arrangement, and required fire detail, stop the substitution review and return the question to the architect or engineer. A nominally similar track is not enough.

Fire-rated and sound-rated partitions need a complete assembly

Slotted track alone does not establish a fire or sound rating. Performance depends on the complete head-of-wall and partition assembly, including wall framing, track, joint width, board system, sealant or joint treatment, fasteners, insulation, and installation details.

A Canadian government renovation specification describes slotted deflection track as tested and certified for use in fire-rated wall construction. Another requires a ULC or cULUS-labelled assembly for slotted track used in fire-rated construction. Review the fire-rated assembly requirement before approving a substitution.

For sound-rated work, confirm that the head joint, sealant, board attachment, and movement detail do not create a rigid bridge or otherwise change the tested wall construction.

Field checklist: preserve the movement after installation

Use this sequence before the partition is closed. The approved drawings, specifications, and rated assembly govern if site conditions differ from the planned detail.

  1. Confirm the latest detail. Check current structural, architectural, mechanical, electrical, and partition drawings for revisions affecting the wall head.
  2. Verify the track orientation. Confirm the correct profile, leg dimensions, slot direction, and location relative to the structure and studs.
  3. Install fasteners only where permitted. A fastener through the wrong part of a slot or through a movement zone can restrict intended travel.
  4. Keep the studs free to move. Do not add screws, clips, welds, blocking, or attachments that lock the stud web or flanges to the structure above unless the detail requires them.
  5. Maintain the specified head gap. Measure the gap at representative locations and correct framing or substrate irregularities before boarding.
  6. Prevent board bridging. Gypsum board should not be fastened so it connects the moving wall head rigidly to the structure above.
  7. Use the specified joint treatment. Sealants, mineral fibre, firestopping, and acoustic treatments must match the approved assembly and joint width.
  8. Inspect before concealment. Record the track, fasteners, gap, board termination, and joint treatment before finishes hide the detail.

Specification and safety note: Where the installed condition conflicts with the approved movement or fire detail, do not solve the conflict by cutting slots, enlarging gaps, or changing fasteners in the field. Have the responsible design professional and approved assembly documentation govern the correction.

What to request in a product submittal or quotation

A useful request should describe the condition, not just ask for “slotted track.” Include the following:

  • Product designation and intended use, including non-load-bearing or structural classification.
  • Track width, leg dimensions, steel thickness or gauge, coating, and available lengths.
  • Slot width, slot length, slot spacing, orientation, and permitted fastener locations.
  • Allowable movement direction and capacity, including limitations on vertical or horizontal movement.
  • Compatible stud profile, stud engagement, framing spacing, and connection method.
  • Required head-of-wall gap and installation tolerance.
  • Fire documentation, such as a tested or labelled assembly, where a fire rating is required.
  • Acoustic documentation or assembly information where sound performance is specified.
  • Installation instructions, drawings, movement tables, and substitution information.
  • Quantities, lengths, packaging, delivery sequence, and project-specific fabrication requirements.

Flag missing movement, rating, or compatibility data before approval. The strongest comparison is not simply the lowest nominal track price. It is the product and documented assembly that match the project’s movement, performance, installation, and procurement requirements.

Questions that resolve the last selection risks

Is slip track the same as slotted deflection track?

Not necessarily. “Slip track” is a broad term often used for a head detail that permits relative movement, while slotted deflection track identifies a particular slotted track arrangement. Confirm the exact product, movement direction, installation method, and tested assembly in the project documents.

Is the deflection track itself slotted, and how do the slots work?

Yes, a slotted deflection track has openings designed to permit movement in the intended direction when installed with the specified fasteners and clearances. The slots must be considered with the gap, stud engagement, track legs, and complete assembly. Slots alone do not define usable movement capacity.

Can slotted deflection track accommodate horizontal drift or seismic movement?

Do not assume it can. Standard vertical deflection track primarily addresses relative vertical movement. Horizontal drift or seismic movement may require a different or combined system with project-specific engineering, cycling, side connections, and fasteners.

How much deflection gap should be left at the head of the wall?

Leave the gap shown in the approved project detail. There is no universal gap value because the required space depends on movement demand, product geometry, installation tolerances, and fire or acoustic joint treatment.

Who determines the required movement capacity for a deflection track detail?

The structural engineer establishes structural movement information, while the architect or responsible design team coordinates partition, head-of-wall, fire, acoustic, and finish requirements. The contractor and supplier verify that the proposed product and installation match those documents before ordering.

Coordinate the detail before you order

Before approving a slotted deflection track, reconcile structural movement, the architectural head detail, wall role, required gap, rated assembly, stud compatibility, and installation method. If any input is missing, the selection is not ready for a confident order.
